vignette:
Sofia is a competent HVAC technician, or at least, she used to be. At twenty-seven, she was proud of her skill with complex machinery and the physical demands of the job. But for the past eight months, that confidence has been eroding, replaced by a constant, humming dread. The turning point was an incident six weeks ago. She was on a routine service call, a simple condenser flush for a client in a suburban townhouse. When a woman answered the door and led her to the basement unit, alone, a cold panic seized Sofia. She found herself staring at the single egress window, calculating escape routes. The client’s friendly questions felt like interrogations. Sofia faked a phone call, mumbled something about needing a specific part from the supply house, and fled, leaving her tools behind. She never went back. The warning from her boss that followed was what finally brought her to therapy.

The event that reshaped her world happened a year ago. During a trip to visit family abroad, she was abducted and held captive for three days. Her captors were two women. They had seemed kind at first, offering her a ride when her car broke down on a rural road. The memory of their betrayal is a constant, chilling reminder that you can never know who will harm you. They kept her in a small, windowless room, her wrists and ankles bound so tightly the friction left raw wounds. She could see the damage they were inflicting, the angry red lines and deep purple bruises, a visual testament to her powerlessness. When she tries to recall the details now, the memory feels strangely distant, like a disturbing film she once saw. It feels like it belongs to someone else, a story about a different woman in a different life. But then, a flash of sensory detail—the smell of stale cigarette smoke, the rough texture of the ropes—will make it feel terrifyingly real. In those moments, a hot wave of shame washes over her, so potent and overwhelming that she has to physically shake her head, focusing on the grout lines of her shower tile or the grain of her kitchen table to stop the memory in its tracks.

Her life is now governed by a new set of rules she can’t seem to break. Her small apartment has become a fortress. Each night, before she can even think about sleep, she must check the lock on her front door, then the latch on each window, then the door again, sometimes three or four times, until her hand is sure the bolt is truly home. Even then, sleep is a temporary reprieve. She often jolts awake in the dead of night, her heart hammering against her ribs, straining her ears for the sound of an intruder, absolutely certain she is not safe. The hypervigilance follows her to work. The sudden clang of a dropped pipe wrench on a concrete floor can make her jump so violently she nearly loses her balance on a ladder. Last week, she saw a coworker with a bandaged hand and felt a dizzying nausea, the image of his minor injury momentarily transposing over the memory of her own wounded wrists.

The job itself, once a source of pride, has become a landscape of potential threats. Crawlspaces and tight attics, which she once navigated with ease, now feel like tombs. The feeling of being cornered, of having no options for a quick exit, triggers a frantic, primal urge to escape. This fear, coupled with her profound distrust of being alone with female clients, has made her work life precarious. She is convinced she has permanently changed for the worse, that the capable, trusting person she once was is gone forever. Every time she flinches at a loud noise or avoids a job, it reinforces a devastating new belief: she can’t trust herself to do the right thing anymore. Sofia came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate, quiet plea to stop her world from shrinking any further.
